query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultra‐thin, high‐temperature oxidation‐resistant ceramic coating (e.g. Y2O3 or Al2O3) on the as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy will improve its long‐term mechanical stability, reduce room‐temperature creep, and enhance corrosion resistance under extreme thermal cycling.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure that exhibits good tensile strength and ductility but shows limitations under long‐term mechanical loading, thermal fluctuations, and corrosive environments.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultra‐thin (sub-micron) protective ceramic coating via a technique such as physical vapor deposition (PVD) to form a uniform Y2O3 or Al2O3 layer over the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Subject coated and uncoated specimens to cyclic thermal exposure (e.g., from –50°C to 700°C), long-duration mechanical loading (creep tests at room and elevated temperatures), and corrosive environments (such as chloride-containing acid or salt spray conditions) to simulate service in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners.
generation.structural_mediator: The protective coating acts as a diffusion and oxidation barrier at the alloy’s surface, minimizing the ingress of reactive species and reducing surface degradation, microcrack initiation, and grain-boundary sliding under prolonged loading.
generation.mechanism: By preventing aggressive environmental attack (oxidation and corrosion) and stabilizing the surface against stress-assisted degradation, the coating limits the initiation of creep and microcracks, thereby preserving the alloy’s intrinsic strength–ductility balance over long-term service.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated alloys, the coated fasteners should exhibit a measurable reduction in creep strain (particularly at room temperature and during cyclic thermal loads) and enhanced resistance to corrosion, leading to improved long-term mechanical stability. The improvement is expected to be significant enough to narrow the gap toward industrial requirements, although the exact magnitude is uncertain.
generation.baseline: Uncoated as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy fasteners currently showing good strength and ductility but insufficient performance under extreme thermal cycling, sustained mechanical loading, and corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold under controlled thermal cycling and corrosive exposure typical of accelerated service tests; however, if the coating adhesion deteriorates under severe mechanical deformation or if the coating imparts detrimental residual stresses, the benefits may be offset.
generation.uncertainty: The durability of the coating adhesion under repeated thermal cycling and long-term mechanical stress is uncertain, as is the precise quantification of improvements in creep resistance and corrosion rate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of fastener specimens from the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy. Apply an ultra-thin ceramic coating (e.g., Y2O3 via PVD) to one set while leaving the other set uncoated as a control. Expose both groups to cyclic thermal loading (–50°C to 700°C), sustained mechanical creep tests at room and elevated temperatures, and corrosion tests in a chloride-containing solution or salt spray environment. Periodically assess the mechanical performance (creep strain, tensile properties), corrosion damage (via weight loss and surface morphology analysis), and coating integrity (via SEM/TEM and adhesion tests).
measurements: Creep strain vs. time under constant load
Corrosion rate (weight loss, pit density, and depth)
Tensile strength and elongation before and after exposure
Coating integrity and adhesion (via microscopy and scratch tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not display statistically significant improvements in reduced creep strain, enhanced corrosion resistance, and better long-term mechanical stability compared to the uncoated controls under identical accelerated test conditions, then the hypothesis—that the protective coating improves the practical performance of the alloy—will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. The high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a new alloy with more than four main elements. In recent years, HEAs have attracted attention due to their outstanding performance, including superior mechanical properties, abrasion resistance, and corrosion resistance [,]. Single-phase body-centered-cubic (BCC) and face-centered-cubic (FCC) HEAs have been the subject of much research over the past decade. Several studies have reported that BCC HEAs possess high strength, while FCC HEAs are highly ductile. According to comprehensive research, it is difficult to achieve both high strength and ductility in single-phase HEAs [,,]. To further improve the properties of HEA, Lu et al. [,] proposed the concept of eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) that combined the strength of BCC HEAs and ductility of FCC HEAs. EHEAs have broad application prospects due to their excellent mechanical properties over a wide temperature range [,,]. However, EHEA research mainly focuses on mechanical properties, while there are few studies on the corrosion behavior of EHEAs.
